# How to use this file

The code is complete, but the **answers to the questions are left blank** for you to work out. Fill each `Your answer` line as we go.

Put `DaphniaAges.txt`, `FlyWings.txt` and `FishMove.txt` in the **same folder** as this `.Rmd` OR your working directory. You can also load it directly from the course website (online loading).

* Daphnia: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/DaphniaAges.txt

* Fly Wings: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/FlyWings.txt

* Cod Movement: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/FishMove.txt

Instructions:

* Run chunk by chunk (green arrow).
* After completing the Lab press **Knit**, select **Knit to PDF** to produce the output, and submit that PDF
* Before you run a block of code, ask yourself: what does this line do, and what do I expect to see?

**The idea of the lab.** ANOVA is the General Linear Model (GLM) with a *categorical* explanatory
variable (a **factor**). Everything you learned in Lab 5 carries over: write the model, run it,
save residuals and fitted values, check the residuals, then test. The general form of the model is

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta \, X + \epsilon_{normal}$$

where:

* $\beta_0$ is the mean of the reference group (e.g., Placebo group)
* $\beta$ is the difference in group mean ($\text{Mean}_{\text{Treatment group}} - \text{Mean}_{\text{Placebo group}}$).

For the Placebo group $X=0$,

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta(0) + \epsilon = \beta_0 + \epsilon$$

For the Treatment Group ($X = 1$),

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta(1) + \epsilon = \beta_0 + \beta + \epsilon$$ 

The straight-line assumption (Assumption 1) does not apply to a factor, so only the three error
assumptions remain: (1) homogeneous, (2) normal and (3) independent residuals.

|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|

## 1.3 The model in GLM format

* What is the symbol for the Response? 

* What is the symbol for the Explanatory ?

Fill in the blanks of  $\_\_\_\_ = \beta_0 + \beta \_\_\_\_ + \epsilon_{normal}$:

where $\beta_0$ = mean of the reference group and $\beta$ =  treatment group mean $-\ \beta_0$).

## 1.4 Define the data from file (tabular format)

The text file has **7 rows and 2 columns**, one column per strain, followed by notes. `nrows = 7` makes R read
only the data. The data is not well organised for group mean comparison. We then name each group (column) *Strain1* and *Strain2*.

```{r daphnia-wide}
# 1. Original wide format
daphnia_wide <- data.frame(
  Strain_I  = c(7.2, 7.1, 9.1, 7.2, 7.3, 7.2, 7.5),
  Strain_II = c(8.8, 7.5, 7.7, 7.6, 7.4, 6.7, 7.2)
)

# 2. Convert to long format using base R stack()
daphnia_long <- stack(daphnia_wide)
names(daphnia_long) <- c("age", "strain")

# 3. Clean up factor labels
levels(daphnia_long$strain) <- c("Strain I", "Strain II")

daphnia_long
```

Now, let's import the true data

```{r d-import}
dfile <- "DaphniaAges.txt"

DaphniaAges <- read.table(dfile, nrows = 7)       # read the 7 data rows
names(DaphniaAges) <- c("Strain1", "Strain2")     # name each group (column)
DaphniaAges                                       # display the input table
Mean_Strain1 <- mean(DaphniaAges$Strain1)
Mean_Strain1
Mean_Strain2 <- mean(DaphniaAges$Strain2)
Mean_Strain2
```

## 1.5 Reorganize from tabular to model format

Some packages can run ANOVA on the tabular format (Minitab: `aovoneway c1-c2`). R's `lm()` needs **model
format**: all values of the response in **one column** and, next to each value, a **label** for its group.

Pseudocode (handout p. 2): place each response value into one column; name it; label a new column for
the explanatory variable; for each Y value, put its category label in the adjacent X column.

```{r d-stack}
Daphnia <- stack(DaphniaAges)        # stack the columns; adds a label column (ind)
names(Daphnia) <- c("Age", "Strain") # name the two new columns: response, factor
Daphnia                              # display the data object (14 rows)
str(Daphnia)                         # Age is numeric; Strain is a factor with 2 levels
```

Line 1 creates a new object (nothing is printed); line 2 renames
columns (nothing printed); line 3 prints the 14 rows. `str()` confirms that `Strain` is a **factor**,
which is exactly what `lm()` needs for ANOVA.

**Why *Strain* is a fixed factor?** The research question was whether these **two known genetic strains**
differ. They are not a random sample from a population of strains, so inference is to these two strains only.

## 1.6 Run the GLM ANOVA and save residuals and fits

Define Y = Age, define X = Strain, write the model and run it, save residuals and fitted values.

```{r d-lm}
DModel <- lm(Age ~ Strain, data = Daphnia)   # the model:  Age = grand mean + strain effect
Dfit <- fitted(DModel)                     # fitted values: the mean of each strain
Dres <- resid(DModel)                      # residuals: observation - its strain mean
summary(DModel)                           # parameter estimates and t-tests
anova(DModel)                                # the ANOVA table (SS, df, MS, F, p)
```

### What do the coefficients mean?

**Intercept and "slope"**

R uses treatment coding by default, setting the first factor level (Strain 1) as the reference baseline.

Strain 1 is the reference (Strain = 0)

Thus, 

$$\text{Mean}_{Age\; strain\; 1} = \beta_0 + \epsilon_{normal}$$

$\text{Parameter StrainStrain2} = 0.0429$ is the difference between the mean of Strain 2 and the mean of Strain 1

$$\text{Mean}_{Age\; strain\; 2} = \text{Parameter StrainStrain2} + \text{Mean}_{Age\; strain\; 1}  + \epsilon_{normal}$$
$$\text{Mean}_{Age\; strain\; 2} = \text{Parameter StrainStrain2} + \text{Mean}_{Age\; strain\; 1} = 0.0429 + 7.5143 = 7.5572$$

```{r calculated-vs-model}
Compare_means <- data.frame(
  rbind(Calculated = c(Mean_Strain1,Mean_Strain2), 
        Model_estimates = c(coef(DModel)[1],coef(DModel)[2]+coef(DModel)[1])
        )
  )
names(Compare_means) <- c("Strain 1","Strain 2")
Compare_means

# Let's look at the mean of each group directly given by GLM
fitted(DModel)
```

**F-ratio**

F-ratio determines whether the difference between averages of strain 1 and strain 2 are meaningful or just the result of random chance.

$$\text{F-ratio} = \frac{\text{Variance between groups}}{\text{Variance within groups}}$$

If F < 1 (Low F): The observed differences is likely due to the natural noise inside the groups.

If F ≈ 1 (Low F): The differences between group averages are about the same size as the natural noise inside the groups. The variation is likely due to random chance.

Large F (e.g., 5, 10, or higher): The differences between group averages are much larger than the noise inside the groups. This indicates that at least one group is genuinely different from the others.

```{r d-ttest}
anova(DModel) # Look at the result first then run
between_group_variance <- anova(DModel)$"Mean Sq"[1]
between_group_variance
within_group_variance <- anova(DModel)$"Mean Sq"[2]
within_group_variance
f_ratio_calculated <- between_group_variance/within_group_variance
f_ratio_calculated
f_ratio <- anova(DModel)$"F value"[1]
f_ratio
model_df <- anova(DModel)$"Df"[1] # $n_parameters/groups - 1 = 2 - 1$
model_df
residual_df <- anova(DModel)$"Df"[2] # Residual degrees of freedom (\text{total observations} - n_groups$) = 14 - 2.
residual_df
p_value <- anova(DModel)$"Pr(>F)"[1]
p_value
```

What type of variance dominates?

> **Answer.** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## 1.7 Evaluate the model: residual diagnostics

**Assumption 1 (straight line).** There is no straight-line model with a factor, so we skip it.
**Assumptions 2a and 2b.** Residuals homogeneous and normal. Plot the residuals against the fitted values and the normal scores.

```{r d-diag, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Daphnia ages: residuals vs fitted values (left) and normal scores plot (right)."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Dfit, Dres, xlab = "fitted values (strain means)", ylab = "residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs fits")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(Dres, main = "Normal scores of residuals")
qqline(Dres)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
tapply(Dres, Daphnia$Strain, sd)       # spread of the residuals in each strain
```

## 1.8 Test, randomization and decision (Lab 6a items A-G)

```{r d-numbers}
c(between_group_variance = between_group_variance,
  within_group_variance = within_group_variance,
  f_ratio = f_ratio, 
  model_df = model_df,
  residual_df = residual_df,
  p_value = p_value)
```

| Step | What to report | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | Model; $H_A$/$H_0$ about the difference in means | &nbsp; |
| B | Test statistic | &nbsp; |
| C | Residual vs fit plot | &nbsp; |
| D | Normality (one graph) | &nbsp; |
| E | Randomization needed? | &nbsp; |
| F | Decision about $H_0$ | &nbsp; |
| G | Decision in words | &nbsp; |

A : Model and $H_A$/$H_0$ about the difference in means
**Your answer:** $Age = \beta_0 + \beta\,Strain + \epsilon$. $H_0$: $\beta = 0$ (the two strain have the same mean). $H_A$: $\beta \neq 0$ (the means differ).

B: Test statistic (Report $F = MS_{among}/MS_{within}$) with the model df and residual df
**Your answer:** $F = 0.006/0.457 = 0.014062$ with 1 and 12 degree of freedom

C: Statement about the Residual vs fit plot
**Your answer:** The Residual vs fit plot is homogeneous (Figure above)

D: Statement about Normality (one graph)
**Your answer:** Residuals are close to the line except two large points

E: Do we need Randomization?
**Your answer:** No. n = 14 is small, but $p$ = 0.91 is nowhere near $\alpha$ = 0.05, so a better $p$-value cannot change the decision.

F: Decision about $H_0$ 
**Your answer:** We do not reject $H_0$

G: State Decision in words 
**Your answer:** There is no evidence that mean age at first reproduction differs between the two strains

# Analysis 2. Random factor ANOVA: fly wing lengths

**Research question.** What is the variance in fly wing length among 7 random samples?
(Data: Table 8.1, Sokal and Rohlf; 7 samples of 5 housefly wing lengths; $WL$ = mm $\times$ 0.1.)

## 2.1 Table of variables (symbols *WL* and *Sample*)

| Variable | Symbol | Units | Scale type | Role |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Wing length | WL | 0.1 mm (mm x 0.1) | ratio | Response |
| Sample (7 random samples) | Sample | none (7 categories) | nominal | Explanatory |

## 2.2 The model in GLM format

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## 2.3 Import and reorganize (modify the code from Analysis 1)

The file has 5 rows and 7 columns: each **column is one sample** of 5 flies. Same steps as Analysis 1:
read, name the groups, stack, rename.

```{r f-import}
ffile <- "FlyWings.txt"
FlyWings <- read.table(ffile, nrows = 5)             # 5 rows x 7 columns (5 observation x 7 groups)
names(FlyWings) <- paste0("Sample", 1:7)             # name each group: Sample1 ... Sample7
Flies <- stack(FlyWings)                             # tabular -> model format
names(Flies) <- c("WL", "Sample")
head(Flies, 10)
str(Flies)                                           # 35 obs.; Sample is a factor with 7 levels
```

## 2.4 Run the model and print the data equations

Pseudocode: values in one column Y; labels in X; calculate the mean of each category; place the mean next
to each Y (the **fits**); calculate $Y - \text{fits}$ (the **residuals**); display
**Data = Fits + Residuals**.

```{r f-lm}
FModel <- lm(WL ~ Sample, data = Flies)   # one-way ANOVA
summary(FModel)
Ffit <- fitted(FModel)                  # the mean of each flies' sample
Fres <- resid(FModel)                   # observation - sample mean
WL <- Flies$WL                        # copy the response into its own vector
DataEq <- cbind(WL, Ffit, Fres)           # Data | Fits | Residuals side by side
DataEq
```

Check that the columns add up (Data = Fits + Residuals):

```{r f-check}
all.equal(unname(WL), unname(Ffit + Fres))   # TRUE: Data = Model + Residual for every fly
```

Pick one wing-length observation and write its data equation:

> **Answer.** First fly: (Data) 41 = (Model mean of Sample1) 43.6 + (Residual) -2.6.

Your turn, pick one,

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Going one step further, the model part splits into the grand mean and the sample effect:

```{r f-split}
# Sample 1 effect
Fgrand <- mean(Flies$WL)
c(grand_mean = Fgrand, sample1_effect = Ffit[1] - Fgrand, residual = Fres[1])
# Sample 2 effect
c(grand_mean = Fgrand, sample2_effect = Ffit[8] - Fgrand, residual = Fres[1])

summary(lm(WL ~ Sample, data = Flies, contrasts = list(Sample = "contr.sum")))
```

Reconstructing Group Means (`contr.sum`)

| Group | Formula ($\text{Grand Mean} + \text{Effect}$) | Calculated Sample Mean |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| Sample 1 | $45.343 + (-1.743)$ | 43.60 |
| Sample 2 | $45.343 + 2.657$ | 48.00 |
| Sample 3 | $45.343 + 1.057$ | 46.40 |
| Sample 4 | $45.343 + (-2.943)$ | 42.40 |
| Sample 5 | $45.343 + (-1.143)$ | 44.20 |
| Sample 6 | $45.343 + 2.057$ | 47.40 |
| Sample 7 | $45.343 + 0.057$ | 45.40 |

Where is sample 7 effect? R does not display it, but it can be calculated from the first 6 effect

Because all group effect mus sum to zero, we calculate it by taking the negative sum of the first 6 effects.

$$\text{Sample7_effect} = -(-1.743 + 2.657 + 1.057 - 2.943 - 1.143 + 2.057) = -(-0.057) = +0.057$$

## 2.5 Why *Sample* is a random factor

The groups were **not formed by named treatments** as in an experiment; the samples were chosen without
regard to any attribute of the group. The research question asks whether groups **differ at all**, and
inference is to the **population the samples were drawn from**, not just the 7 samples measured.
For a random factor the null hypothesis is about a **variance**, not about specific means.

## 2.6 Evaluate the model

```{r f-diag, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Fly wing lengths: residuals vs fitted values (left) and normal scores plot (right)."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Ffit, Fres, xlab = "fitted values (sample means, 0.1 mm)", ylab = "residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs fits")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(Fres, main = "Normal scores of residuals")
qqline(Fres)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
round(tapply(Fres, Flies$Sample, sd), 2)      # spread within each sample
```

Do you see any strong heterogeneity in the residual vs fit plot?

## 2.7 Test, variance components and decision

```{r f-anova}
# 1. Run ANOVA table on the 7-level model
anova_table <- anova(FModel)
anova_table
# 2. Extract variances (Mean Squares)
flies_between_group_variance <- anova_table$"Mean Sq"[1]  # MS_Sample (MS between groups)
flies_within_group_variance  <- anova_table$"Mean Sq"[2]  # MS_Residuals (MS within groups)

# 3. Calculate and extract F-ratio
flies_f_ratio_calculated <- flies_between_group_variance / flies_within_group_variance
flies_f_ratio            <- anova_table$"F value"[1]

# 4. Extract degrees of freedom
flies_model_df <- anova_table$"Df"[1]  # k - 1 = 7 groups - 1 = 6
flies_residual_df <- anova_table$"Df"[2]  # N - k = 35 - 7 = 28

# 5. Extract p-value
flies_p_value <- anova_table$"Pr(>F)"[1]

# 6. Combine into a named vector
results_vector <- c(
  between_group_variance = flies_between_group_variance,
  within_group_variance  = flies_within_group_variance,
  f_ratio                = flies_f_ratio, 
  model_df               = flies_model_df,
  residual_df            = flies_residual_df,
  p_value                = flies_p_value
)
print(results_vector)
```

# Analysis 3. ANOVA in model format: cod movements

The data are from Don Clark (Memorial University), used with permission. The data illustrate several
perplexities: should we treat **time as a regression variable or as a factor**? What if we cannot trust the
$p$-values because of gross violations of assumptions? Is randomization worth the effort?

## 3.1 Read the structure of the file

The information about the structure is at the **bottom** of the file: the variates are distances (m) moved
by tagged cod in 10 successive 2-minute periods at each of 12 times of day. The first column is the time
group (1 to 12), the second the distance.

```{r fish-import}
mfile <- "FishMove.txt"
FishMove <- read.table(mfile, nrows = 120)       # 120 rows: 12 times x 10 periods
names(FishMove) <- c("Time", "Dist")             # time group, distance moved (m)
str(FishMove)                                    # Time was read as integer (numeric)
head(FishMove)
```

State a research question (Look at the end of the file online):
Copy paste in your browser or look in your downloaded data
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/FishMove.txt


Research Question:
> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## 3.2 Time: regression variable or factor?

To decide, plot Distance against Time. `Time` is currently numeric, so R draws a scatterplot.

```{r fish-scatter, fig.cap="Cod movement (distance per 2-minute period) against time-of-day group, with the mean of each group."}
with(FishMove, plot(Time, Dist, xlab = "Time of day (group 1 = dawn ... 12)",
                    ylab = "Distance moved (m)",
                    main = "Cod movement vs time of day"))
means_by_time <- tapply(FishMove$Dist, FishMove$Time, mean)
lines(1:12, means_by_time, col = "red", lwd = 2)            # the mean of each time group
```

Why is fitting a trend (regression line) inappropriate?

> **Answer.** The pattern is not a straight line: movement is high at dawn, low in mid-morning, high again around group 6, low again, then highest at the end (a repeating up-and-down pattern). A line cannot follow it, so a regression would wrongly say time does not matter.

Now fit the straight-line regression (Time still numeric) and look at the result:

```{r fish-regression}
anova(lm(Dist ~ Time, data = FishMove))   # Time still numeric: a straight-line regression
```

## 3.3 Table of variables and model

| Variable | Symbol | Units | Scale type | Role |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Distance moved per 2-minute period | Dist | m | ratio | Response |
| Time of day (groups 1-12, from dawn) | Time | group code (hours after dawn) | nominal (12 categories) | Explanatory |


Use your symbols to write the model in GLM format:

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## 3.4 Convert numbers to a factor and run the GLM ANOVA

R reads `Time` as numeric because every entry is a number. To treat it as **categories**, convert it
to a factor with `as.factor()`:

```{r fish-factor}
FishMove$Time <- as.factor(FishMove$Time)   # numeric -> factor (12 levels)
str(FishMove)
```

The same `plot()` call now draws **boxplots**, because Time is a factor:

```{r fish-boxplot, fig.cap="Cod movement by time-of-day group (boxplots), after Time was converted to a factor."}
with(FishMove, plot(Time, Dist, xlab = "Time of day (group 1 = dawn ... 12)",
                    ylab = "Distance moved (m)", main = "Distance by time group"))
```

Define Y; define X; execute the model and save residuals and fitted values; check the
$p$-value assumptions (homogeneous, normal residuals).

```{r fish-lm}
CModel <- lm(Dist ~ Time, data = FishMove)
Cfit <- fitted(CModel)
Cres <- resid(CModel)
anova(CModel)
summary(CModel)$r.squared     # proportion of variance explained by time of day
```

## 3.5 Residual diagnostics

```{r fish-diag, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Cod movement: residuals vs fitted values (left) and normal scores plot (right)."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(Cfit, Cres, xlab = "fitted values (mean distance, m)", ylab = "residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs fits")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(Cres, main = "Normal scores of residuals")
qqline(Cres)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
round(tapply(FishMove$Dist, FishMove$Time, sd), 2)    # SD of each time group
cor(Cfit, abs(Cres))                                  # does spread grow with the mean?
```

Are the residuals homogeneous?

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Are the residuals normal?

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## 3.6 Is randomization worth the effort?

Having checked the residuals, we ask: could a better $p$-value change the decision?
We can check by randomization (Lab 4 method): shuffle the time labels, recompute $F$, and see how often shuffled data give an $F$ as large
as the observed one.

```{r fish-rand}
nrep <- 2000
C_F <- anova(CModel)$"F value"[1]
C_P <- anova(CModel)$"Pr(>F)"[1]
F_random <- replicate(nrep, anova(lm(Dist ~ sample(Time), data = FishMove))$"F value"[1])
c(F_observed = C_F, p_F_distribution = C_P,
  p_randomization = mean(F_random >= anova(CModel)$"F value"[1]), shuffles = nrep)
```


```{r fish-rand-plot, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Randomization distribution of F (2000 reshuffles). The red line is the observed F."}
hist(F_random, breaks = 30, xlim = c(0, max(C_F, F_random) * 1.05),
     xlab = "F from reshuffled data", main = "Randomization distribution of F")
abline(v = C_F, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```


## 3.6 Anova table and key parameters

```{r cod-anova-table}
# 1. Run ANOVA table once and store it
cod_anova <- anova(CModel)

# 2. Extract variances (Mean Squares)
cod_between_group_variance <- cod_anova$"Mean Sq"[1]  # MS between
cod_within_group_variance  <- cod_anova$"Mean Sq"[2]  # MS within (residuals)

# 3. F-ratio
cod_f_ratio_calculated <- cod_between_group_variance / cod_within_group_variance
cod_f_ratio <- cod_anova$"F value"[1]

# 4. Degrees of freedom
cod_model_df <- cod_anova$"Df"[1]
cod_residual_df <- cod_anova$"Df"[2]

# 5. P-value
cod_p_value <- cod_anova$"Pr(>F)"[1]

# 7. Combine into a named vector
cod_results <- c(
  between_group_variance = cod_between_group_variance,
  within_group_variance  = cod_within_group_variance,
  f_ratio_calculated     = cod_f_ratio_calculated,
  f_ratio                = cod_f_ratio,
  model_df               = cod_model_df,
  residual_df            = cod_residual_df,
  p_value                = cod_p_value
)
print(cod_results)
```

| Step | What to report | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | Model; $H_A$/$H_0$ | &nbsp; |
| B | Test statistic | &nbsp; |
| C | Residual vs fit | &nbsp; |
| D | Normality (one graph) | &nbsp; |
| E | Randomization needed? | &nbsp; |
| F | ANOVA table; decision | &nbsp; |
| G | Decision in words | &nbsp; |

# Lab 6b : find your own data and apply the 10-step recipe

This is not required

**Task:** Find data presented in **at least three categories of a single explanatory variable**.
Display the data in **model format**, showing the variable names and the first 10 lines. List the **full
reference** for the source of the data. Then present the analysis using the **10-step generic recipe
for hypothesis testing with the General Linear Model**.

## Where to find data: the references on the course website

The course website keeps a file of references to articles that display data
([RefswithDataForGeneralLinearModels.txt](https://github.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/blob/main/Data/RefswithDataForGeneralLinearModels.txt)).
The file has three sections: references for models with 2 factors (3 references), 3 factors (1 reference) and
miscellaneous GLMs (a longer list; see the file). The multi-factor references are:

**Refs with data for GLM with 3 factors (3-way ANOVA)**

1. Berven, K.A. and Grudzien, T.A. (1990). Dispersal in the wood frog (*Rana sylvatica*): implications for genetic population structure. *Evolution* 44: 2047-2056.

**Refs with data for GLM with 2 factors (2-way ANOVA)**

1. Boyd, J.T. (1960). Climate, air pollution, and mortality. *British Journal of Preventive and Social Medicine* 14: 123-135.
2. Eberhardt, L.L. (1978). Transect methods for population studies. *Journal of the Wildlife Management* 42: 1-31.
3. Heitman, H., et al. (1958). Ambient air temperature and weight gain in swine. *Journal of Animal Science* 17: 62-67.

For Lab 6b you need only **one** explanatory variable with 3 or more categories: pick one factor from the
article (or one table of data), and ignore the other factors. Articles published before 1980 display raw
data more often than recent ones. Check the handout rule: use the **full reference** (authors, year, title,
journal, volume, pages).

## What is the 10-step generic recipe?

The recipe is Dr. Schneider's *Generic Recipe* for inference with the General Linear Model
(Part 3 lecture notes,
[GenericRecipe2019.pdf](https://www.mun.ca/biology/schneider/b4605/LNotes/Pt3/GenericRecipe2019.pdf)).

| Earlier lab | What it gave you | Recipe steps |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Lab 2 (Equations) | Table 2.1: a 6-step recipe to translate and use an equation (symbols, units, words, estimates, calculation) | 1 (write the model) |
| Lab 3 (Distribution functions) | $p$-values from $t$, $F$, $\chi^2$ | 6-7 |
| Lab 4 (Randomization) | Table 4.1: recipe for a randomization test | 8 |
| Lab 5 (Regression) | model, residual diagnostics, likelihood ratio, $F$-test, "do we need to recompute the $p$-value?", effect size | 1-4, 6-10 |

### The 10 steps, one by one

| # | Step | What you do | R |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Construct the model | State the question, identify **response** vs **explanatory** variable(s), their units and scale, and write the model | `Y = b0 + b X + e` |
| 2 | Execute the model | Put the data in model format, code the model, compute fits and residuals | `stack()`, `lm()`, `fitted()`, `resid()` |
| 3 | Evaluate with residuals | Check homogeneity, normality and independence. If a problem, go back to step 1 | `plot(fit, res)`, `qqnorm()`, `lag.plot()` |
| 4 | Partition df and SS | Write the full model and the reduced (null) model; sums of squares and df for each term; likelihood ratio | `anova()` |
| 5 | Define the target of inference | Decide what you want to say: strength of evidence, a decision at a fixed error rate, or an update of prior belief | (a decision) |
| 6 | State the test statistic and its distribution | $F$, $t$, $\chi^2$, or Monte Carlo (randomization) | (a statement) |
| 7 | Build the ANOVA table | Mean squares, $F$-ratio, $p$-value (Type I error) | `anova()`, `pf()` |
| 8 | Recompute the $p$-value if necessary | Only if assumptions fail, the sample is small (< 30) and $p$ is near $\alpha$ | `replicate()`, `sample()` |
| 9 | Report the statistical conclusion | Reject or not reject $H_0$; ANOVA table, factor contrasts | `anova()`, `summary()` |
| 10 | Report the science conclusion | Biologically meaningful parameters (means, slopes) with one measure of uncertainty (SE, SD or CI) | `tapply()`, `confint()` |

**Step 1 - Construct the model.** Before touching software, say in words what you are asking and which variable
is the response (plotted on Y) and which is the explanatory variable (the factor). Write the model
$Y = \beta_0 + \beta X + \epsilon$. *Lab link:* the "table of variables" you filled in at the start of every analysis.

**Step 2 - Execute the model.** Reorganize the data to model format and fit it with `lm()`. Save the fitted values
(the model part) and the residuals (the leftover). *Lab link:* `stack()` + `lm()` in Analysis 1.

**Step 3 - Evaluate the model using residuals.** The $p$-value you will get in step 7 is only trustworthy if the
residuals are homogeneous, independent and about normal. For a factor there is no straight-line assumption.
If the residuals fan out (as for the cod data), a plain ANOVA may not be the right model.

**Step 4 - Partition df and SS.** Compare two models: the *full* model ($Y = \beta_0 + \beta X$) and the
*reduced* null model ($Y = \beta_0$, no factor). The SS the factor explains is the difference. The likelihood
ratio $LR = (1 - r^2)^{-n/2}$ from Lab 5 measures how much more likely the data are under the full model.

**Step 5 - Define the target of inference.** Three styles exist. *Evidential:* how strongly do the data favour
one model over another (the LR). *Frequentist:* a decision at a fixed Type I error ($\alpha$ = 0.05).
*Priorist:* update prior beliefs. In these labs we mainly use the first two.

**Step 6 - State the test statistic.** For ANOVA it is $F = MS_{among}/MS_{within}$, with $df_1$ = number of
groups $-$ 1 and $df_2$ = $n$ $-$ number of groups. It can be compared with the $F$ distribution (Lab 3) or with a
randomization distribution (Lab 4).

**Step 7 - Build the ANOVA table.** Sums of squares divided by df give mean squares; the ratio is $F$; `pf()`
turns it into a $p$-value, the probability of an $F$ at least this large if $H_0$ were true.

**Step 8 - Recompute the Type I error if necessary.** Randomization is extra work, so do it only when it could
matter: assumptions violated **and** small sample **and** $p$ close to 0.05 (Lab 5's "do we need to recompute the
$p$-value?" box, and the Box 3 questions).

**Step 9 - Report the statistical conclusion.** "We reject / do not reject $H_0$", with $F$, df, $p$ and the ANOVA table.
Remember: you can reject $H_0$, not "accept $H_A$".

**Step 10 - Report the science conclusion.** Translate back to biology: which groups are higher or lower, by how
much (means or contrasts) and with what uncertainty (SE, SD or CI).

### Worked example: the 10 steps applied to the cod data

**Step 1 - Model.** Question: does cod movement depend on time of day? Response *Dist* (m, ratio);
explanatory *Time* (12 categories, nominal). Model $Dist = \beta_0 + \beta\,Time + \epsilon_{normal}$.

**Steps 2 - 3 - Execute and evaluate.** Done in Analysis 3 (`CModel`, `Cfit`, `Cres`): residuals are **not** homogeneous and **not** normal.

**Step 4 - Partition SS and df (full vs reduced model).**

```{r r4}
Cod_LR <- (1 - summary(CModel)$r.squared)^(- nrow(FishMove) / 2)
reduced <- lm(Dist ~ 1, data = FishMove)      # H0 model: one grand mean, no time effect
anova(reduced, CModel)                        # compares reduced vs full: same F as anova(CModel)
c(r_squared = summary(CModel)$r.squared, n = nrow(FishMove), LR = Cod_LR)   # LR = (1 - r^2)^(-n/2)
```

The LR formula uses only $r^2$ and $n$; it does not penalise the 11 extra parameters, so compare it with the $p$-value
rather than reading it alone.

**Step 5 - Target of inference.** We make a frequentist decision at $\alpha$ = 0.05 and report the LR as supporting evidence.

**Step 6 - Test statistic.** $F = MS_{Time}/MS_{residual}$ with 11 and 108 df (compared with the $F$ distribution and, in step 8, a randomization distribution).

**Step 7 - ANOVA table.**

```{r r7}
anova(CModel)
pf(anova(CModel)$"F value"[1], 11, 108, lower.tail = FALSE)          # p-value by hand from the F distribution
```

**Step 8 - Recompute the $p$-value if necessary.** The assumptions fail, but n = 120 is not small and $p$ is far
from 0.05. The randomization we ran in Analysis 3 gave $p$ < 0.0005, in agreement, so the decision stands.

**Step 9 - Statistical conclusion.** $F_{11,108}$ = 4.76, $p$ = 6.2 x 10$^{-6}$: reject $H_0$ (all 12 time-group means are equal).

**Step 10 - Science conclusion.** Report the group means with an uncertainty measure.

```{r r10, fig.cap="Mean distance moved (+/- 1 SE) by time-of-day group."}
Cmean <- tapply(FishMove$Dist, FishMove$Time, mean)
Cse   <- tapply(FishMove$Dist, FishMove$Time, function(x) sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)))
round(rbind(mean = Cmean, SE = Cse), 2)
# contrast of each group from the grand mean (sum-to-zero coding, as in the lab's definition of beta)
round(Cmean - mean(Cmean), 2)

mid <- barplot(Cmean, ylim = c(0, max(Cmean + Cse) * 1.15), xlab = "Time of day (group 1 = dawn ... 12)",
               ylab = "Mean distance moved (m)")
arrows(mid, Cmean - Cse, mid, Cmean + Cse, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04)
```

Movement is highest at dawn (about 11.7 m) and in the last group (12.8 m), with a second peak at group 6 (11.1 m), and lowest around groups 3 and 9 (about 2.8 m). Because the residuals are right-skewed and heterogeneous, the
group means (especially those at the peaks, with SE of 2.4-3.3 m) are imprecise; a transformation or a
model with non-normal errors (Lab 10, GLMs) could be explored.
